content: Althaea is a genus that comprises between six and twelve species of perennial herbs, including the marshmallow plant, which is the origin of the name for the confectionery treat. These plants are native to Europe and western Asia. They typically grow along riverbanks and in salt marshes, thriving in moist, sandy soils. The stems of Althaea species can reach heights of 1 to 2 meters and produce flowers during mid-summer. The leaves are palmately lobed, with three to seven distinct lobes. Certain species of Lepidoptera larvae, such as Bucculatrix quadrigemina, use Althaea plants as a food source. Historically, the genus Althaea included additional species that are now classified under the genus Alcea, commonly known as hollyhocks. The roots of Althaea plants are rich in various compounds, including 37% starch, 11% mucilage, 11% pectin, flavonoids, phenolic acids, sucrose, and asparagine. In herbal medicine, mallow (a common name for Althaea species) is used as a gargle to treat ulcers in the mouth and throat. It is also considered beneficial for managing gastric ulcers. The flowers and young leaves of the plant are edible and are often incorporated into salads or prepared by boiling or frying. Additionally, these parts of the plant are used in cosmetics for skin care. The root of the marshmallow plant has been utilized since ancient Egyptian times in a honey-sweetened confection that was used to soothe sore throats. A later French adaptation of this recipe, known as pâte de guimauve, incorporated egg white meringue and was often flavored with rose water. This preparation more closely resembles modern commercially available marshmallows, which, ironically, no longer contain any actual marshmallow plant material.
